hints: Notice the student has the same mass and climbs to the same classroom, so the vertical height $h$ is identical for running and walking.
Connect that height to gravitational potential energy using $E_p = mgh$, which depends on $m$, $g$ and $h$ but not on speed or time.
Connect the time difference to power using $P = W/t$, where the work done against weight is the same but $t$ is smaller when running.
walkthrough: Identify what is the same: the student's weight $mg$ and the vertical height $h$ of the stairs to the classroom are unchanged whether she runs or walks.
State the rule for energy: gain in gravitational potential energy is $E_p = mgh$. Since $m$, $g$ and $h$ are the same, the energy gained is the same.
State the rule for power: power is the rate of doing work, $P = W/t$, where $W$ is approximately the work done against gravity.
Compare the times: running takes a smaller time $t$ than walking to transfer the same energy $W$.
Conclude that dividing the same $W$ by a smaller $t$ gives a larger $P$, so running uses more power for the same energy gain. This is option C.

options.A: The height gained is the same, so $mgh$ is the same. Only the time changes, not the final gravitational potential energy.
options.B: The gravitational potential energy is not larger when running, and delivering the same energy in less time cannot mean the same power.
options.C: The same mass raised through the same height gains the same $mgh$, but the shorter time when running gives larger $P = W/t$.
options.D: The energy gained is the same, but the power is not the same because running takes less time to do the same work.
